messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Malik was eight years old when he first learned how silence could mean something terrible was about to happen. He was standing in the hallway of his family’s apartment, one hand pressed flat against the wall, the other clamped over his own mouth so his mother wouldn’t hear him cry. The living room was quiet—a heavy, waiting silence that pressed against his ears. Then his father’s voice, low and grinding, and then the sound of something hitting the wall. Malik remembers that moment as a picture in his mind: the crack in the plaster, the overturned lamp, his mother’s face turned away. He remembers his own body, frozen behind the door, arms locked at his sides, every muscle rigid. Even now, when a memory of that night comes back, his body goes into that exact position—shoulders hunched, breath held, as if he is still hiding. And the grief that follows is overwhelming, a bottomless sadness for his mother that feels as fresh as it did a decade ago.

As Malik grew older, the feeling of helplessness hardened into a belief: first, that he could not stop bad things from happening to people he loved, but deeper still, that he could not stop bad things from happening to him either. He had stood there and done nothing, and nothing had protected him. The thought lodged itself quietly: *Bad things can find me, and I can't do anything about it.* He began to scan every room for danger before he could feel safe—noticing where a knife sat on a counter, how a stranger’s hand rested near his pocket, the way a person’s eyes moved when they spoke. By the time he became a police officer at eighteen, that vigilance felt like an asset. He told himself he would be the one who saw the threat first, who would never be caught off guard again.

But the job has made everything worse. Malik now spends his shifts in unfamiliar houses, hallways, basements—places whose layouts he cannot predict, where danger could be in any corner. Every call feels like stepping into that hallway again. When he enters a home and the residents go silent, his heart slams against his ribs because he knows that silence: it means something is about to break. He sees potential weapons everywhere—a beer bottle on a coffee table, a screwdriver on the kitchen counter—and his eyes lock onto them before he can even hear what the dispatcher is saying. He has come to believe that he cannot rely on himself to stay calm. More than once, his partner has had to touch his shoulder to get his attention during a quiet scene, and Malik has flinched hard, his hand flying to his holster. That unexpected touch, when he is not prepared for it, sends a jolt through his whole body—the same jolt he felt when his father’s fist connected with the wall near his mother’s head. And underneath that jolt lives a quieter certainty: *Something bad is going to happen to me, and I won't be able to stop it.*

Malik has started to avoid places he does not already know. Off-duty, he stays mostly at home. He will not go to a new restaurant or a friend’s apartment unless he can visit it first in daylight, alone, to map the exits. He tells himself he needs to assess the danger, but the logic feels thin. What frightens him most is the feeling that his own mind is no longer trustworthy—that his reactions since that night mean he is going crazy. He has never told anyone about the snapshots that intrude at random moments: his mother’s flinch, the frame of the door, the crack in the plaster. When they come, his body acts as if it is still there, and he has to excuse himself from the room to stand in the hallway alone until the feeling passes. The helplessness he felt as a boy—the certainty that he could not protect himself—has never left. It follows him into every unfamiliar room, every quiet moment, every split second when his hand moves toward his holster before his mind can catch up.

What finally brought Malik to seek help was a domestic violence call three weeks ago. He walked into a living room, saw a woman with her arm raised protectively across her face, and he stopped cold. His body locked into that childhood position—arms at his sides, breath stopped—and he could not move or speak. His partner handled the situation, but afterward Malik sat in the squad car shaking, flooded with grief and the old helplessness. The old certainty pressed in: *I can't stop bad things from happening to me.* He is afraid that he will freeze again on a call and someone will get hurt. He is afraid that his captain will notice, that he will be seen as unfit. But underneath that, he is hoping that someone can explain why a memory that is ten years old still has hold of his body, and whether there is a way to let go.
